3	A CSV parser, streaming parser and serializer for Node.js with no dependencies.
4	It follows RFC 4180 and also accepts LF and CR line breaks and a leading byte
5	order mark.
6	
7	```js
8	const { parse, createParser, stringify, CsvError } = require('csv-rfc4180');
9	
10	parse('name,age\r\nAda,36\r\n');
11	// [['name', 'age'], ['Ada', '36']]
12	
13	parse('name,age\nAda,36\n', { header: true });
14	// [{ name: 'Ada', age: '36' }]
15	
16	stringify([['a', 'b,c'], ['say "hi"', '']], { eol: '\n' });
17	// 'a,"b,c"\n"say ""hi""",\n'
18	```
19	
20	## API
21	
22	### `parse(text, options = {})`
23	
24	Parses a whole string and returns an array of records. Each record is an array
25	of strings, or an object keyed by the first record's fields when `header` is
26	`true`.
27	
28	| Option           | Default | Meaning                                                           |
29	| ---------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
30	| `delimiter`      | `','`   | One character other than `"`, CR or LF.                           |
31	| `header`         | `false` | Use the first record as column names and return objects.          |
32	| `skipEmptyLines` | `false` | Drop empty lines instead of returning them as `['']`.             |
33	
34	Throws `TypeError` when `text` is not a string or an option is invalid, and
35	`CsvError` when the input is malformed.

40	the same options as `parse`. `write` returns the records completed by that
41	chunk; `end` returns whatever is left. Records and errors are the same as
42	`parse` would give for the whole input, however the chunks split it. Once
43	`end()` has run or either method has thrown, both methods throw an `Error`.
44	
45	```js
46	const parser = createParser({ header: true });
47	parser.write('id,note\n1,"multi'); // []
48	parser.write('\nline"\n2,x');      // [{ id: '1', note: 'multi\nline' }]
49	parser.end();                      // [{ id: '2', note: 'x' }]
50	```
51	
52	Each character is read once and only the record in progress is kept, so time
53	and memory grow linearly with the input.

# csv-rfc4180

A CSV parser, streaming parser and serializer for Node.js with no dependencies.
It follows RFC 4180 and also accepts LF and CR line breaks and a leading byte
order mark.

```js
const { parse, createParser, stringify, CsvError } = require('csv-rfc4180');

parse('name,age\r\nAda,36\r\n');
// [['name', 'age'], ['Ada', '36']]

parse('name,age\nAda,36\n', { header: true });
// [{ name: 'Ada', age: '36' }]

stringify([['a', 'b,c'], ['say "hi"', '']], { eol: '\n' });
// 'a,"b,c"\n"say ""hi""",\n'
```

## API

### `parse(text, options = {})`

Parses a whole string and returns an array of records. Each record is an array
of strings, or an object keyed by the first record's fields when `header` is
`true`.

| Option           | Default | Meaning                                                           |
| ---------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `delimiter`      | `','`   | One character other than `"`, CR or LF.                           |
| `header`         | `false` | Use the first record as column names and return objects.          |
| `skipEmptyLines` | `false` | Drop empty lines instead of returning them as `['']`.             |

Throws `TypeError` when `text` is not a string or an option is invalid, and
`CsvError` when the input is malformed.

### `createParser(options = {})`

Returns `{ write(chunk), end() }` for input that arrives in pieces. It takes
the same options as `parse`. `write` returns the records completed by that
chunk; `end` returns whatever is left. Records and errors are the same as
`parse` would give for the whole input, however the chunks split it. Once
`end()` has run or either method has thrown, both methods throw an `Error`.

```js
const parser = createParser({ header: true });
parser.write('id,note\n1,"multi'); // []
parser.write('\nline"\n2,x');      // [{ id: '1', note: 'multi\nline' }]
parser.end();                      // [{ id: '2', note: 'x' }]
```

Each character is read once and only the record in progress is kept, so time
and memory grow linearly with the input.

### `stringify(rows, options = {})`

Serializes an array of records, each an array of values, and ends the output
with one `eol`. Strings are written as is, numbers and booleans with
`String()`, and `null` or `undefined` as an empty field. Any other value
throws `TypeError`.

| Option      | Default  | Meaning                                                                    |
| ----------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `delimiter` | `','`    | Validated as in `parse`.                                                   |
| `eol`       | `'\r\n'` | `'\r\n'` or `'\n'`.                                                        |
| `header`    | none     | Array of column names. Written first; object records are read in its order. |

A field is quoted when it contains the delimiter, `"`, CR or LF, or begins or
ends with a space. A record made of a single empty field is written as `""` so
it survives `skipEmptyLines`. For rows that are non-empty arrays of strings,
`parse(stringify(rows, opts), opts)` returns the same rows.

### `CsvError`

Subclass of `Error` with 1-based `line` and `column` properties. Columns count
UTF-16 code units. The message ends with the position, for example
`Unclosed quoted field (line 3, column 7)`.

| Problem                                   | Reported position                             |
| ----------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Quoted field never closed                 | Its opening `"`                               |
| Character after a closing `"`             | That character                                |
| Duplicate header name                     | Start of the second occurrence's field        |
| Wrong field count in header mode          | Line where the record starts, column 1        |

When the input has several problems, the first one met reading left to right
is thrown. A record's field count is checked when the record ends.

## Behavior worth knowing

- Line numbers count every line break, including those inside quoted fields,
  with CRLF counting as one.
- A leading BOM is removed before counting, so the first character after it is
  column 1.
- In `createParser`, a record ended by a CR is returned right away. If the next
  chunk begins with LF, that LF completes the CRLF and does not add an empty
  record.
- A `__proto__` column in header mode becomes an ordinary own property of each
  record.
- `stringify` quotes the first field when the output would otherwise begin with
  a BOM, since `parse` would drop it.
- `stringify([], { header })` writes the header row alone.
- `stringify` reads only an object's own properties, so an inherited key counts
  as missing.
- Unknown options are ignored, so one options object can be passed to both
  `parse` and `stringify`.

## Tests

```sh
npm test
```

Uses the built-in `node:test` runner (Node 18 or later).

`parse` and `createParser` now take `trim` and `comment`, and the full suite passes (105 tests). I haven't committed anything.

- **`trim`:** removes spaces and tabs from both ends of unquoted fields. It also allows them before an opening `"` and after a closing `"`, keeps the quoted content exactly, and still treats a field with spaces before its opening quote as quoted. A space or tab delimiter is never trimmed. A `"` in the middle of an unquoted field stays ordinary. Any other character after a closing quote, once the spaces and tabs are skipped, is the same error as before.
- **`comment`:** only the first character of a line can start a comment, so the character inside a multi-line quoted field or after leading spaces is ordinary. A comment line is skipped with its CR, LF or CRLF, and it isn't an empty line and never becomes a record, even before the header. Bad values throw `TypeError`, and line numbers in errors still count comment lines.
- **Chunk splitting:** both options run in the same character-by-character parser as everything else, so `createParser` matches `parse` wherever the input is split.

The spec left a few points open. I chose these, and the README now documents them:
- A line of only spaces or tabs is not empty. With `trim` it becomes a record with one empty field, so `skipEmptyLines` keeps it.
- An unclosed quote is reported at the `"`, not at the spaces before it.
- A duplicate header name is reported at the start of its field, spaces included.

**Tests:** I added `trim` and `comment` suites to `test/parse.test.js` for defaults, validation, both options' rules, error positions and the header. In `test/stream.test.js` I added the new option combinations to the split-point, byte-by-byte and seeded-random checks. I also added new corpus entries, `#` and tab in the random alphabet, and a few streaming and validation cases.

The changes are in `src/csv.js`, the two test files and `README.md`.
